name: Brimonidine gel (Mirvaso)

lead: Mirvaso is a 0.33% brimonidine tartrate gel, approved by the FDA in 2013 for the facial redness of rosacea, that visibly reduces redness within hours of application. It was described at launch as the first drug aimed at the hallmark redness of the condition.

Brimonidine is an alpha-2 adrenergic agonist, in medical use since 1996 for eye conditions. It activates receptors in the skin's blood vessels, causing them to constrict so less blood shows at the surface. Rosacea overviews place the peak effect at roughly 3 to 6 hours after application, and the effect is temporary.

paras: People apply it to the face as a daily gel under a prescription, often timed before events or work since the effect peaks hours after application. It is used alongside other rosacea care such as sunscreen and anti-inflammatory creams.

Reported adverse effects include flushing or redness worse than baseline, allergic contact dermatitis, severe rebound erythema in case reports, and one reported case of symptomatic bradycardia. It is prescription-only in many countries.

angle.text: Brimonidine gel narrows facial blood vessels so less blood shows near the surface, visibly reducing rosacea redness within hours. The effect is temporary, and the product has had FDA approval for this use since 2013. Rebound redness has been reported in some users.

lead: Brimonidine gel (Mirvaso, brimonidine tartrate 0.33%) was approved by the US FDA in 2013 for facial erythema of rosacea and was described at launch as the first drug aimed at the hallmark redness of the condition [1]. Brimonidine is an alpha-2 adrenergic agonist, first patented in 1972 and in medical use since 1996 for eye conditions [2].

Rosacea overviews describe brimonidine as constricting vessels to reduce redness, with a peak effect 3 to 6 hours after application [2]. A review of facial erythema in rosacea places the redness in the context of immune dysregulation and neurovascular dysfunction [3].
Published case reports describe adverse reactions including allergic contact dermatitis [4][5], rebound erythema [6][1] and a case of symptomatic bradycardia [7].

paras: The gel is indicated for persistent facial redness of rosacea in adults [1][2]. The same ingredient appears in ophthalmic products for glaucoma and ocular redness, some available over the counter in the US [2].

A 2014 Drug and Therapeutics Bulletin appraisal and a SkinMed product summary reviewed the product at launch [8][9]. A small imaging study used optical coherence tomography to monitor treatment response [10]. Registered post-marketing studies include open-label studies of 101 and 205 participants and a 301-person utilisation and satisfaction survey [11][12][13]; results are not summarised here. Because the effect is a vessel constriction, rosacea references describe it as reducing redness during the hours of effect rather than altering the disease [2].

Commonly reported adverse events include redness or flushing worse than baseline, most often with the first application [1]. Case reports describe a paradoxical erythema reaction with long-term use [1], severe rebound erythema labelled dermatitis medicamentosa [6], and allergic contact dermatitis, including sensitisation in two cases [4][5]. A 2024 case report described symptomatic bradycardia after use [7]. Systemic effects of brimonidine in other forms include low blood pressure and dry mouth [2].
Brimonidine constricts blood vessels through alpha-2 adrenergic activation, which in the skin reduces redness [2].

Human studies include open-label post-marketing trials in rosacea [11][12], a utilisation study [13] and a small imaging study [10]. Studies in other conditions (hand-foot syndrome, flushing in aldehyde dehydrogenase deficiency) are registered but concern other uses [14][15].
The gel is mentioned in skincare circles as an option for temporary redness before events, typically alongside discussion of rebound redness reports.

timeline.event: FDA approves Mirvaso gel 0.33% for facial erythema of rosacea. [1]
